hints: Think about what the bottom box labelled elements means. Arrows going up from elements to reactants and to products represent formation of each compound from its elements.
Recall the Hess Law expression that links reaction enthalpy to formation enthalpies, remembering to multiply each value by its balancing number in the equation.
walkthrough:
Picture the Hess cycle correctly**
You have reactants on the left, products on the right, and elements underneath. Going up from elements to make the reactants is formation of reactants. Going up to make the products is formation of products. By Hess Law, the direct route $\Delta H_{r}$ plus one formation route must equal the other formation route, so $\Delta H_{r} = $ formation of products minus formation of reactants.

Multiply by the balancing numbers**
This is where most slips happen. You do not just add one of each value. Look at the equation: $\text{K}_{2}\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7} + 4\text{KCl} + 3\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4} \rightarrow 2\text{CrO}_{2}\text{Cl}_{2} + 3\text{K}_{2}\text{SO}_{4} + 3\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. So sum for products is $$2(-580) + 3(-1438) + 3(-286) = -6332 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ and sum for reactants is $$(-2061) + 4(-437) + 3(-814) = -6251 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$.

Subtract and finish with units**
Now apply the formula: $$\Delta H_{r} = -6332 - (-6251) = -81 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$. The negative sign tells you the reaction is slightly exothermic. Always include the sign and the unit $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Final answer: $\Delta H_{r} = \Sigma \Delta H_{f}^{\ominus}(products) - \Sigma \Delta H_{f}^{\ominus}(reactants)$
$= [2(-580) + 3(-286) + 3(-1438)] - [(-2061) + 4(-437) + 3(-814)]$
$= -81 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Look at the formula $[\text{Cr}(\text{NH}_{3})_{4}\text{Cl}_{2}]^{+}$. It is octahedral with two identical $\text{Cl}$ ligands that can be arranged differently in space.
walkthrough:
Spot the two identical ligands**
Chromium here is 6 coordinate, so the shape is octahedral. You have four $\text{NH}_{3}$ and two $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ligands. The two $\text{Cl}$ ligands can sit next to each other at $90^{\circ}$ or opposite each other at $180^{\circ}$.

Name that arrangement**
When the same two ligands can be cis to each other or trans to each other, that is cis-trans isomerism, also called geometrical isomerism. One isomer of $[\text{Cr}(\text{NH}_{3})_{4}\text{Cl}_{2}]^{+}$ is cis and the other is trans.

hints: Start by recalling what happens to the five 3d orbitals when ligands approach the central $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ ion in an octahedral field.
Think about how a coloured complex interacts with white light, and what happens to a d electron when a photon is taken in.
Remember that the colour you see is the light that is not absorbed, it is transmitted or reflected.
Consider why swapping $\text{Cl}$ from cis to trans positions might change the energy absorbed even though the ligands are the same.
walkthrough:
Split the d orbitals**
Free $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ has five 3d orbitals at the same energy. When six ligands approach octahedrally, they repel the d electrons unequally. The orbitals pointing directly at ligands are raised in energy and those pointing between ligands are lowered. So you get two sets: a lower set and a higher set separated by an energy gap, $\Delta E$.

Absorb light to jump the gap**
$\text{Cr}^{3+}$ is $3\text{d}^{3}$, so there are vacancies in the upper set. A d electron in the lower set can absorb a photon whose energy exactly matches $\Delta E$ and be promoted to the upper set. This is a d-d transition. Because $\Delta E$ corresponds to photons in the visible region, part of white light is absorbed.

Link absorption to observed colour**
What you see is not what is absorbed. If yellow light is absorbed, the remaining red and blue light reaches your eye and you see violet, and vice versa. So the complex appears coloured because it selectively absorbs one colour from white light.

Explain why cis and trans differ**
Both isomers contain the same metal and same ligands, but the spatial arrangement of $\text{NH}_{3}$ versus $\text{Cl}^{-}$ around chromium is different. $\text{NH}_{3}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ exert different field strengths, so the exact splitting pattern and the size of $\Delta E$ is slightly different for cis-$[\text{Cr}(\text{NH}_{3})_{4}\text{Cl}_{2}]^{+}$ compared with trans-$[\text{Cr}(\text{NH}_{3})_{4}\text{Cl}_{2}]^{+}$. A different $\Delta E$ means a different frequency and wavelength is absorbed, so the complementary colour left over is different. That is why one is green and the other is violet.

Final answer: In the complex the 3d orbitals are split into two energy levels.
Colour arises because visible light is absorbed to promote a d electron from the lower to the higher d level (d-d transition).
The unabsorbed wavelengths are transmitted / reflected and seen as colour.
The cis and trans arrangements split the d orbitals by a different amount, so a different wavelength is absorbed and different colours are observed.
